persona.name: Savitha Das
persona.background: She runs a small shop and has been feeling increasingly tired at work, needing frequent breaks. She has noticed her abdomen feels fuller than before, making long hours of standing uncomfortable.

diagnoses.name: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), BCR-ABL1 positive
diagnoses.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by overproduction of myeloid cells with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly; Philadelphia chromosome/BCR-ABL1 fusion is present in >95% and LAP/NAP score is decreased.

diagnoses.name: Primary myelofibrosis
diagnoses.description: A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm with fibrotic marrow; peripheral smear shows leukoerythroblastosis with tear drop cells and nucleated red cells; LAP score is raised and Philadelphia chromosome is negative.

diagnoses.name: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
diagnoses.description: An acquired clonal stem cell disorder with progressive cytopenias and dysplasia in ≥10% of cells of any one myeloid lineage; may present with weakness, infections, or hemorrhage due to cytopenias.

diagnoses.name: Megaloblastic anemia (vitamin B12/folate deficiency)
diagnoses.description: Macrocytic anemia with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; may have leukopenia and thrombocytopenia with markedly increased LDH and indirect bilirubin.

diagnoses.name: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
diagnoses.description: A diagnosis of exclusion characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (often <80 × 10^9/L) with mucocutaneous bleeding; splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are uncommon.

diagnoses.name: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
diagnoses.description: An acquired hemolytic anemia with features of intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria) and pancytopenia; NAP score is reduced and diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 deficiency.

diagnoses.name: Hairy cell leukemia
diagnoses.description: A B-cell leukemia in middle-aged to elderly patients with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia; peripheral smear shows characteristic hairy cells and bone marrow aspirate often yields a dry tap with fibrosis.

diagnoses.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
diagnoses.description: A chronic leukemia of mature-looking lymphocytes, typically >50 years, with fatigue, weight loss/anorexia, painless generalized lymphadenopathy, and sometimes splenomegaly/hepatomegaly.

diagnoses.name: Hodgkin lymphoma
diagnoses.description: A lymphoma where peripheral blood may show normocytic normochromic anemia, eosinophilia (~20%), and sometimes thrombocytosis; staging incorporates B symptoms (fever >38°C, night sweats, weight loss).

diagnoses.name: Hemolytic anemia
diagnoses.description: Anemia due to increased RBC destruction with reticulocytosis; may have jaundice, splenomegaly (extravascular hemolysis), and increased LDH; intravascular hemolysis can cause hemoglobinuria.

relevantFindings:
Examination: Pallor. Moderate to massive, nontender splenomegaly; mild hepatomegaly may be present. Possible sternal tenderness/bone pain. Laboratory: Hemoglobin usually <11 g/dL. Total leukocyte count markedly raised, almost always >20,000/µL and often >100,000/µL. Peripheral smear: normocytic normochromic anemia; WBC shows left shift with granulocytes at all stages of development (neutrophils, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, promyelocytes, occasional myeloblasts) with blasts usually <10%; increased basophils (<20%) and eosinophils. Platelets may be normal/increased/decreased (automated counts can be falsely elevated due to granulocyte disruption). Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular due to hyperplasia of granulocytic elements; late stages may show fibrosis. Decreased NAP/LAP score (usually <20) helpful to differentiate from leukemoid reaction. Philadelphia chromosome positive in >95%; BCR-ABL1 fusion gene demonstrable by cytogenetics/RT-PCR/FISH. Biochemistry: increased LDH and uric acid; increased serum alkaline phosphatase; markedly elevated serum vitamin B12 due to transcobalamin production by granulocytes.

redHerrings: Intermittent mild night sweats could suggest lymphoma (Hodgkin lymphoma staging uses B symptoms). Occasional easy bruising could suggest ITP or MDS, though bleeding tends to occur late in CML and ITP typically has isolated thrombocytopenia without leukocytosis. A brief episode of darker urine could suggest intravascular hemolysis/PNH, but the key discriminators here are marked leukocytosis with left shift and low NAP/LAP with Philadelphia chromosome positivity.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)** is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the **BCR-ABL1** fusion (Philadelphia chromosome), causing uncontrolled granulocytic proliferation. It typically presents with marked leukocytosis, anemia-related symptoms, and **splenomegaly** from extramedullary hematopoiesis, and can progress to **blast crisis** resembling acute leukemia.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Anemia from marrow crowding reduces oxygen delivery, causing persistent tiredness over months.
**Pallor** - Visible sign of low hemoglobin, supporting chronic anemia typical in CML presentation.
**Left-sided abdominal fullness** - Suggests enlarged spleen; **splenomegaly** is common due to extramedullary hematopoiesis.
**Moderate to massive nontender splenomegaly** - Classic CML finding; reflects disease burden and sequestration of blood cells.
**Bone pain / sternal tenderness** - Due to hypercellular marrow expansion and periosteal irritation in myeloproliferation.
**Bleeding not prominent early** - Thrombocytopenia/platelet dysfunction usually occurs later, so early minimal bleeding fits CML.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The combination of chronic fatigue and pallor indicates anemia, while a heavy/full sensation in the left abdomen strongly suggests **splenomegaly**, a hallmark of CML. CML typically shows markedly elevated WBC counts with a **left shift** (granulocytes at all maturation stages) and increased **basophils/eosinophils**, with blasts usually <10% in chronic phase. A low **LAP/NAP score** helps distinguish CML from a leukemoid reaction, and confirmation is by **Philadelphia chromosome**/**BCR-ABL1** detection via cytogenetics, FISH, or RT-PCR. The described possibility of progression to **blast crisis** (>30% blasts) aligns with known CML transformation patterns.

precomputedExplanations.description: Primary myelofibrosis is a **BCR-ABL1–negative myeloproliferative neoplasm** characterized by clonal megakaryocytic proliferation with progressive **bone marrow fibrosis** and extramedullary hematopoiesis. It typically presents with anemia, constitutional symptoms, and **massive splenomegaly**, and shows a leukoerythroblastic blood picture with tear-drop cells.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Anemia-related reduced oxygen delivery causes persistent tiredness and decreased exercise tolerance.
**Pallor** - Low hemoglobin produces pale skin and mucosa, often accompanied by tachycardia.
**Splenic fullness** - Enlarged spleen causes left upper quadrant heaviness and early satiety symptoms.
**Bone pain** - Marrow expansion and periosteal irritation can cause sternal tenderness or deep aches.
**Constitutional symptoms** - Cytokine-driven fever, night sweats, and weight loss may occur in advanced disease.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: Primary myelofibrosis can resemble CML because both can cause **anemia** and **splenomegaly** from extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, PMF classically produces a **leukoerythroblastic** smear (nucleated RBCs, early myeloid forms) with prominent **tear-drop cells** and often progressive cytopenias. In contrast, this case’s described laboratory pattern (marked leukocytosis with granulocytes at all maturation stages, low **LAP/NAP**, and **BCR-ABL1/Philadelphia chromosome positivity**) is characteristic of **CML** rather than PMF.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient’s expected findings strongly support **CML**: very high WBC with a granulocytic left shift, **low LAP/NAP**, and **BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia) positivity**. Primary myelofibrosis is typically **BCR-ABL1–negative** and is defined by a leukoerythroblastic smear with tear-drop cells and marrow fibrosis, which are not the emphasized findings here.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **BCR-ABL1/Philadelphia chromosome** - PMF is usually negative; CML is positive in >95% and drives disease biology.
**Peripheral smear pattern** - PMF shows leukoerythroblastosis with **tear-drop cells**; CML shows granulocytes at all stages with basophilia.
**LAP/NAP score** - PMF does not characteristically show markedly decreased LAP; CML typically has **low LAP/NAP**.
**Bone marrow appearance** - PMF has prominent **reticulin/collagen fibrosis** and atypical megakaryocytes; CML is hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia.
**Basophilia** - Basophils are not a defining hallmark in PMF; CML commonly has **basophilia** (can rise markedly, especially in acceleration).
missingFindings: **Tear-drop cells (dacrocytes)** - Their absence argues against the classic leukoerythroblastic picture of PMF.
**Leukoerythroblastic smear** - Lack of nucleated RBCs and marked poikilocytosis makes PMF less likely.
**Bone marrow fibrosis** - No mention of reticulin/collagen fibrosis, which is central to PMF diagnosis.
**BCR-ABL1 negativity** - PMF requires exclusion of **BCR-ABL1–positive** disease; this case supports BCR-ABL1 positivity.
**Atypical megakaryocytic proliferation** - PMF typically shows clustered, atypical megakaryocytes not described here.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)** is a clonal stem-cell disorder causing ineffective hematopoiesis and cytopenias despite a usually cellular marrow. It predominantly affects older adults and may progress to **acute myeloid leukemia (AML)**, but typically presents with low blood counts rather than marked leukocytosis.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Due to anemia from ineffective erythropoiesis, causing reduced oxygen delivery to tissues.
**Pallor** - Visible manifestation of anemia, often accompanying exertional dyspnea and reduced exercise tolerance.
**Recurrent infections** - From neutropenia and dysfunctional neutrophils, leading to frequent bacterial or fungal infections.
**Easy bruising/bleeding** - From thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, causing petechiae, gum bleeding, or epistaxis.
**Constitutional symptoms** - Weight loss or low-grade fever may occur but are not defining features.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: MDS is considered when chronic cytopenias occur with evidence of dysplasia in one or more myeloid lineages. Typical labs show anemia (often macrocytic), leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia, and a peripheral smear with dysplastic forms rather than a pronounced left shift. Bone marrow is usually hypercellular with ineffective maturation, and blasts are increased only in higher-risk subtypes (but not typically with extreme leukocytosis). Splenomegaly can occur but is usually mild and not a dominant early feature.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient’s picture is dominated by **marked leukocytosis with left-shifted granulocytes at all maturation stages**, **basophilia**, **low LAP/NAP**, and **massive nontender splenomegaly**, which strongly supports **CML** rather than MDS. MDS typically presents with **cytopenias** (often leukopenia) and dysplasia, not WBC counts often >100,000/µL with a myeloproliferative smear pattern.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **White blood cell pattern** - MDS usually has normal/low WBC; **CML** has very high WBC with marked **left shift**.
**Basophilia** - Prominent **basophilia** supports **CML**; it is not a typical hallmark of MDS.
**Splenomegaly** - Massive, nontender **splenomegaly** is classic for **CML**; MDS usually has absent/mild splenic enlargement.
**LAP/NAP score** - MDS has no characteristic low LAP pattern; **CML** classically shows **decreased LAP/NAP**.
**Molecular marker** - **BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome)** defines **CML**; MDS lacks **BCR-ABL1** and shows different cytogenetic abnormalities.
**Peripheral smear morphology** - MDS shows dysplasia (e.g., hypogranular neutrophils, pseudo–Pelger-Huët); **CML** shows myeloid precursors across stages with fewer dysplastic features.
missingFindings: **Persistent cytopenias** - MDS requires chronic cytopenia(s); this case emphasizes extreme leukocytosis instead.
**Dysplastic morphology** - Expected dysgranulopoiesis/dyserythropoiesis (e.g., pseudo–Pelger-Huët, ring sideroblasts) is not described.
**Macrocytosis** - MDS commonly causes macrocytic anemia; this case notes **normocytic normochromic anemia**.
**Typical MDS marrow report** - MDS diagnosis relies on marrow dysplasia and blast percentage stratification; findings here fit myeloproliferation.
**Absence of BCR-ABL1** - To support MDS, **BCR-ABL1** should be negative; this case is **Philadelphia chromosome positive**.

precomputedExplanations.description: Megaloblastic anemia is a **macrocytic anemia** caused by impaired DNA synthesis from **vitamin B12** or **folate** deficiency. It produces ineffective erythropoiesis with **macro-ovalocytes** and **hypersegmented neutrophils**, and may cause neurologic deficits in B12 deficiency.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Reduced oxygen delivery from anemia causes persistent tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance.
**Pallor** - Decreased hemoglobin leads to pale skin and mucous membranes on examination.
**Glossitis** - Smooth, sore tongue can occur due to epithelial turnover impairment.
**Paresthesias** - B12 deficiency may cause numbness/tingling from demyelinating neuropathy.
**Gait instability** - Posterior column dysfunction in B12 deficiency causes ataxia and imbalance.
**Mild jaundice** - Ineffective erythropoiesis can raise unconjugated bilirubin causing subtle icterus.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient’s fatigue and pallor could initially suggest anemia, including megaloblastic anemia. However, the dominant additional feature is a sense of left-sided abdominal fullness consistent with **moderate to massive splenomegaly**, which is not typical for isolated B12/folate deficiency. The provided laboratory pattern for this case (marked **leukocytosis** with a **left-shifted granulocytic series**, **basophilia**, low **LAP/NAP score**, and **BCR-ABL1** positivity) strongly indicates **chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)** rather than a nutritional macrocytic anemia.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: Megaloblastic anemia does not explain **massive nontender splenomegaly** with **marked leukocytosis** and granulocytes at all maturation stages. The case’s defining diagnostic evidence is **Philadelphia chromosome/BCR-ABL1** positivity, which is specific for **CML** and unrelated to vitamin deficiency.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **CBC pattern** - Megaloblastic anemia shows **macrocytosis** with low/normal WBC; **CML** shows very high WBC with left shift.
**Peripheral smear** - Megaloblastic anemia has **macro-ovalocytes** and **hypersegmented neutrophils**; **CML** has myelocytes/metamyelocytes, basophilia, and occasional blasts (<10%).
**Splenomegaly** - Usually absent or mild in megaloblastic anemia; often **moderate to massive** in **CML** due to extramedullary hematopoiesis.
**Bone marrow** - Megaloblastic anemia shows **megaloblastic erythroid hyperplasia**; **CML** shows **marked hypercellularity** with granulocytic hyperplasia.
**Diagnostic marker** - No clonal cytogenetic marker in nutritional anemia; **CML** is defined by **BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome)**.
**LAP/NAP score** - Not characteristically low in megaloblastic anemia; typically **decreased** in **CML** (helps distinguish from leukemoid reaction).
missingFindings: **Macrocytosis (high MCV)** - Expected in megaloblastic anemia; case instead emphasizes leukocytosis and myeloid left shift.
**Hypersegmented neutrophils** - Classic smear clue for megaloblastic anemia; case describes granulocytes at all stages and basophilia.
**Low vitamin B12/folate levels** - Biochemical confirmation is required; case provides **BCR-ABL1** positivity instead.
**Neurologic deficits** - B12 deficiency often causes neuropathy/ataxia; case highlights splenomegaly and marrow-related bone pain.
**Reticulocytopenia with ineffective erythropoiesis** - Typical for megaloblastic anemia; case points to myeloproliferation with very high WBC.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)** is an autoimmune disorder in which IgG antibodies target platelet membrane antigens, leading to splenic platelet destruction. It typically presents with isolated thrombocytopenia causing mucocutaneous bleeding, while red and white cell lines are otherwise normal.
keySymptoms: **Petechiae/purpura** - Nonblanching skin spots from low platelets causing superficial capillary bleeding.
**Epistaxis** - Recurrent nosebleeds due to impaired primary hemostasis from thrombocytopenia.
**Gingival bleeding** - Gum bleeding with brushing or spontaneously from platelet deficiency.
**Menorrhagia** - Heavy menstrual bleeding due to reduced platelet plug formation.
**Easy bruising** - Disproportionate ecchymoses after minor trauma because platelets are low.
**Mucosal bleeding** - Oral or gastrointestinal mucosal oozing typical of platelet disorders.
**Isolated thrombocytopenia** - Low platelets with otherwise normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts.
**Normal spleen size** - Spleen is usually not massively enlarged in typical primary ITP.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: ITP is primarily a **platelet destruction** disorder, so the hallmark is **isolated thrombocytopenia** with prominent **mucocutaneous bleeding** (petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding). The peripheral smear in ITP generally shows reduced platelets (often large/young platelets) without a marked **left shift** or major leukocytosis. Splenomegaly is typically absent or mild; massive, nontender splenomegaly suggests an alternative diagnosis. Therefore, the overall pattern expected in ITP does not align with a myeloproliferative picture.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient’s dominant findings are **fatigue/anemia** and **moderate to massive, nontender splenomegaly**, which are not typical of ITP. The case description strongly supports **marked leukocytosis with left-shifted granulocytes** and **BCR-ABL1 positivity**, pointing to **Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)** rather than isolated thrombocytopenia.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary abnormal cell line** - ITP affects **platelets only**; **CML** is a **myeloproliferative neoplasm** with granulocytic proliferation.
**White blood cell count** - ITP has normal WBC; **CML** shows **marked leukocytosis** often >100,000/µL.
**Peripheral smear** - ITP shows low platelets with otherwise normal maturation; **CML** shows **left shift** with granulocytes at all stages and **basophilia/eosinophilia**.
**Splenomegaly** - ITP usually has no/mild splenomegaly; **CML** commonly has **moderate to massive splenomegaly**.
**Genetics** - ITP has no defining cytogenetic marker; **CML** is **Philadelphia chromosome/BCR-ABL1 positive**.
**Enzyme score** - ITP has no characteristic **LAP/NAP** pattern; **CML** classically has **decreased LAP/NAP score**.
missingFindings: **Prominent mucocutaneous bleeding** - Typical ITP presents with petechiae/purpura/epistaxis; bleeding is not prominent early here.
**Isolated thrombocytopenia** - ITP requires thrombocytopenia as the primary abnormality; this case emphasizes anemia and leukocytosis.
**Normal/near-normal spleen size** - Massive, nontender splenomegaly argues against primary ITP.
**Normal leukocyte differential** - ITP should not show a granulocytic left shift or basophilia seen in CML.

precomputedExplanations.description: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (**PNH**) is an acquired clonal stem-cell disorder caused by **PIGA** mutation leading to loss of **GPI-anchored** complement regulators (**CD55/CD59**) on blood cells. This results in complement-mediated **intravascular hemolysis**, cytopenias, and a high risk of **venous thrombosis** (often in unusual sites).
keySymptoms: **Dark/cola-colored urine (morning hemoglobinuria)** - Nocturnal complement activation causes intravascular hemolysis and morning pigmenturia.
**Fatigue** - Hemolytic anemia reduces oxygen delivery, producing chronic tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance.
**Jaundice** - Increased heme breakdown elevates bilirubin, causing scleral icterus and yellowing skin.
**Abdominal pain** - Thrombosis or smooth-muscle dystonia from free hemoglobin can cause episodic abdominal pain.
**Dysphagia/erectile dysfunction** - Nitric oxide scavenging by free hemoglobin causes smooth-muscle spasm symptoms.
**Venous thrombosis** - Hypercoagulability leads to hepatic/portal/cerebral vein thrombosis and related complications.
**Pancytopenia/infections** - Marrow failure overlap can cause neutropenia with recurrent infections and fever.
**Easy bruising/bleeding** - Thrombocytopenia may cause mucosal bleeding, petechiae, or prolonged bleeding.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient’s presentation is dominated by **massive, nontender splenomegaly**, marked **leukocytosis with left shift**, and marrow **granulocytic hypercellularity**, which strongly indicates a **myeloproliferative neoplasm** rather than hemolytic anemia. **CML** classically shows very high WBC counts with granulocytes at all maturation stages, **basophilia**, low **LAP/NAP**, and **BCR-ABL1** positivity. In contrast, **PNH** is primarily a hemolysis/thrombosis syndrome with cytopenias and hemoglobinuria, not a disorder causing extreme granulocytic leukocytosis and massive splenic enlargement. Therefore, PNH does not explain the core hematologic pattern described.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This case describes findings typical of **CML**: very high **total leukocyte count** with **left shift**, **basophilia**, and **massive splenomegaly**, plus **BCR-ABL1** positivity. **PNH** would instead center on **intravascular hemolysis** (dark urine, high LDH with low haptoglobin) and often **cytopenias**, not marked granulocytic leukocytosis.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary mechanism** - **PNH**: complement-mediated hemolysis from loss of **CD55/CD59**; **CML**: **BCR-ABL1** tyrosine kinase–driven myeloproliferation.
**CBC pattern** - **PNH**: anemia with possible leukopenia/thrombocytopenia; **CML**: marked **leukocytosis** with myeloid left shift and variable platelets.
**Peripheral smear** - **PNH**: nonspecific hemolysis features; **CML**: granulocytes at all stages, **basophilia/eosinophilia**, blasts usually <10% in chronic phase.
**Splenomegaly** - **PNH**: not typically massive; **CML**: often **moderate to massive splenomegaly** from extramedullary hematopoiesis.
**Key diagnostic test** - **PNH**: flow cytometry showing reduced **CD55/CD59** (or FLAER); **CML**: **Philadelphia chromosome**/**BCR-ABL1** by PCR/FISH/cytogenetics.
**Major complications** - **PNH**: **hepatic/portal/cerebral venous thrombosis**; **CML**: progression to **accelerated phase/blast crisis** (AML/ALL-like).
missingFindings: **Hemoglobinuria (dark morning urine)** - Typical hallmark of **PNH**; absence makes PNH unlikely here.
**Evidence of intravascular hemolysis** - Expected: high LDH, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia; not described.
**Unusual-site venous thrombosis** - **PNH** commonly causes hepatic/portal/cerebral vein thrombosis; not reported.
**Flow cytometry loss of CD55/CD59 (or FLAER deficiency)** - Required to confirm **PNH**; not present in case data.
**Predominant cytopenias** - **PNH** often shows pancytopenia/aplastic anemia overlap; case emphasizes extreme leukocytosis.

differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Compare features: CML has markedly raised TLC usually >20,000/µL, very low LAP, Philadelphia chromosome positive; myelofibrosis typically has TLC <20,000/µL, leukoerythroblastosis with tear drop cells, dense marrow fibrosis, high LAP, and Philadelphia chromosome negative.

differentialDiagnoses.name: Acute leukemia (AML/ALL) / CML blast crisis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Assess blast percentage and clinical transformation: blast crisis resembles acute leukemia; marrow blasts rise to 20% in blast crisis; FAB mentions transformation when peripheral smear and bone marrow show >30% cells.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Blast crisis phase: It resembles acute (myeloid or lymphoid) leukemia”; phase table: “BM Blasts… Blast crisis 20%”; “Peripheral smear and bone marrow showing >30% cells disease transforms into acute… leukemia.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Suspect CML in a 40–60-year-old with insidious onset of fatigue/weakness and symptoms of massive splenomegaly. On examination, look for pallor and moderate-to-massive nontender splenomegaly (± mild hepatomegaly, sternal tenderness/bone pain). Start with CBC with differential and platelet count, then confirm characteristic peripheral smear (left shift with granulocytes at all stages, blasts usually <10%, basophilia/eosinophilia). Use NAP/LAP score (typically low) to help distinguish from leukemoid reaction. Perform bone marrow study for marked hypercellularity with granulocytic hyperplasia. Confirm diagnosis by demonstrating Philadelphia chromosome and/or BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (cytogenetics; if Ph-negative, use cytogenetics/RT-PCR/FISH; detect BCR-ABL1 in peripheral blood or bone marrow). Differentiate from myelofibrosis using TLC, smear pattern (tear drop cells/leukoerythroblastosis), marrow fibrosis, LAP score, and Philadelphia chromosome status; assess for blast crisis/acute leukemia by blast percentage and transformation features.
